title: Serialization
objectives: Understand serialization via a real-life analogy
Distinguish SGTIN, SGLN, SSCC + other serialized identifiers

sections.markdown:
**Think of serialization as issuing a passport number to every individual physical unit.**

A GTIN says WHAT the product is; a **serial** says WHICH INDIVIDUAL BOX. Combined, they form an **SGTIN** — Serialized GTIN — uniquely identifying every physical unit worldwide.

- **Regulatory driver** — pharma + medical + high-value goods MUST serialize per DSCSA, EU FMD, India CDSCO.
- **Anti-counterfeit** — serials + server-side verification catch fakes.
- **Traceability** — each unit's chain of custody visible via EPCIS events.
- **Recall precision** — 'recall SGTIN X' vs. 'recall entire batch' saves huge waste.

Serial number strategies:
- **Sequential** — simple, predictable, but exposes production volume + easy for attackers to guess.
- **Random** — unpredictable, harder to guess, requires uniqueness check on generation.
- **UUID-shaped compact** — 20-char alphanumeric fits AI (21) max length.
- **Cryptographic (HMAC-based)** — serial embeds a signature; verifiable without server call.

**Why every regulated Flutter app deals with serialization:** printing serials on packaging is one problem; storing + querying billions of them is another; verifying + reporting them is a third. Get any wrong + compliance breaks.

**Serialization** in GS1 = assigning a unique **serial number** to each individual physical unit. Combined with a GS1 key (GTIN → SGTIN, GLN → SGLN, ...) via **AI (21)** (or embedded in URN structure). Serials are up to 20 alphanumeric characters (AI 21 constraint). Governed by brand-owner assignment policies + regulator uniqueness requirements. Central concept in DSCSA, EU FMD, India CDSCO, UDI, and consumer anti-counterfeit flows.

## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: Reusing serials.** Same (GTIN, serial) across products = trace + compliance broken.
**Mistake 2: Predictable sequential without volume-hiding.** Competitors count your daily output.
**Mistake 3: Not enforcing DB uniqueness.** Concurrent generators emit dup serials.
**Mistake 4: Very long serials.** AI (21) allows up to 20 chars; DataMatrix + print quality suffer with long serials.
**Mistake 5: Ignoring EPC URN format.** SGTIN URNs have specific structure; misformed URNs break EPCIS validation.
**Mistake 6: Serial with special characters not in AI (21) allowed set.** GS1 restricts to A-Z, 0-9, and a few specific chars.
**Mistake 7: No expiry / decommissioning event.** Serials pile up in the active set forever.
**Mistake 8: HMAC key in code.** Same issue as any secret — extract from APK; server-side signing only.
## Best practices
**1. Never reuse (GTIN, serial)** for at least 4 years post-decommissioning.
**2. Random or HMAC-based** for anti-counterfeit; sequential OK for internal ops.
**3. DB unique constraint (gtin, serial).**
**4. Partition namespace** by plant + year to avoid coordination overhead.
**5. Length ≤ 20 chars; prefer 12-16** for print + scan reliability.
**6. AI (21) allowed character set enforced.**
**7. HMAC signing on server** — never client.
**8. Decommissioning events** close active-set.

## Interview Q&A

**Q1: Sequential vs random serials — trade-offs?**

**A:** **Sequential (1, 2, 3, ...):** simple, easy to debug + audit, low DB coordination overhead. **Costs:** exposes production volume ('the sequence advanced by 10 million overnight = 10 M units produced'); attackers guess valid serials for counterfeit. **Random:** uniform distribution; unpredictable; counterfeit resistant. **Costs:** requires DB uniqueness enforcement; slightly higher generation cost; harder to audit ordering. **Hybrid:** partition-then-sequential (plant × year × sequence) — hides overall volume while keeping per-partition ordering. **HMAC-based:** serial IS the signature; verify authenticity by re-signing + comparing. **Rule:** consumer-facing anti-counterfeit → random or HMAC; internal ops → sequential OK. Interviewer signal: knowing the volume-exposure risk.

**Q2: What's the AI (21) constraint + how do you build a compliant serial?**

**A:** AI (21) allows **up to 20 characters** from a restricted alphabet: uppercase A-Z, digits 0-9, and characters `!"%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?_` (see GS1 spec for the exact set). No spaces + no lowercase in standard forms. **Case sensitivity:** treated as case-sensitive per GS1 spec. **In practice:** most brands use `A-Z0-9` only (safer across encoding pipelines). **Length:** 12-16 chars balances entropy with DataMatrix print + scan reliability. **Encoding:** in DataMatrix, longer serials = more modules = bigger code. **Interview trap:** using lowercase or specific special chars that break some scanners' decode paths.

**Q3: How do you prevent serial-number collisions in a multi-plant global brand?**

**A:** Options: **(1) Central serial issuance service** — one authority allocates blocks to plants; strong consistency but coordination overhead + single point of failure. **(2) Partitioned namespace** — each plant/year prefix carves out a range; independent generation; no coordination. Recommended for scale. **(3) UUID-based** — each generator emits UUIDs; DB constraint dedups; theoretical collision probability negligible. **(4) Distributed monotonic** (Snowflake ID pattern) — 64-bit counter with plant + time + sequence; each plant has unique bits. **(5) DB unique constraint (GTIN, serial)** as the last line of defense in every strategy; on conflict, retry with new value. **Real-world:** partitioned namespace + DB constraint is the sweet spot. Interviewer signal: recognizing this as distributed-systems territory.

**Q4: What does decommissioning mean + why does it matter?**

**A:** A serialized unit's LIFECYCLE has a start (commissioning at manufacture) + steps (shipping, receiving, storage) + END (decommissioning). **Decommissioning triggers:** dispense to patient, sold to consumer, destroyed, returned + destroyed, expired. **Why matters:** (1) Active set stays bounded (avoids linear growth). (2) Recall investigation ignores already-dispensed. (3) Re-scans of decommissioned serials = counterfeit signal. (4) Regulator reports include lifecycle status. **EPCIS event:** ObjectEvent with `bizStep=dispense` + `disposition=sold` or similar. **After decommissioning:** the serial should NOT reappear in the active supply chain; if it does, alert. **Reuse policy:** GS1 recommends never reusing the same (GTIN, serial) for at least 4 years post-decommissioning; some regulators require longer. **Interviewer red flag:** thinking serials 'exist forever' without a lifecycle model.

**Q5: How does HMAC-based serial verification work?**

**A:** **Idea:** each serial doubles as a cryptographic signature. Server signs `HMAC(counter || GTIN || timestamp, secret_key)` → truncate to 16 chars → serial. **Verification:** scanner extracts (GTIN, serial); calls verification service; server re-signs the same input + compares. **Advantages:** (1) Offline verification possible if scanner has the key (usually undesirable). (2) Counterfeit resistant — attacker can't forge without the key. (3) No DB lookup needed for existence check. **Costs:** (1) Key management — rotate + protect. (2) All serials signed by the same key; key compromise = mass forgery. (3) 16 chars from HMAC → 62^16 collision probability negligible but non-zero. **Alternative:** hybrid — random serial + HMAC signature stored separately + verified server-side. **Pharma flows** rarely use HMAC standalone; they use random + server database + regulator API for defense in depth.

**Q6: How would you architect serial issuance + tracking at scale?**

**A:** **(1) Serialization Service** — REST API that issues serials in bulk (block of 10K per request). **(2) Namespace partitioning** — plant × year × sequence bits ensures no coordination. **(3) DB unique constraint (GTIN, serial)** as final defense. **(4) Async event pipeline** — issued serials emitted as commissioning ObjectEvents to EPCIS repo. **(5) Regulator submission** — dispense events pushed to regulator API. **(6) Anti-counterfeit API** — consumer scans → server lookup + one-time redemption logic. **(7) Data retention** — 7-10 years per regulator; cold-tier storage after 1 year. **(8) Monitoring** — issuance rate, collisions, unusual patterns. **(9) Load model** — plants issue ~thousands per minute; server issues millions per hour peak. **(10) Client SDK** — plants call serialization service; get block; use offline until block exhausted. Interviewer respect: recognizing scale + distributed-systems concerns.

## Real-world usage

- **Pharma DSCSA / CDSCO / FMD** — serialization mandatory for prescription drugs.
- **Medical devices** — UDI (Unique Device Identification).
- **Luxury goods** — anti-counterfeit + provenance.
- **Wine + spirits** — bottle-level serialization.
- **Cold chain** — serialized biologics.
- **NOT ideal for** — low-value FMCG (batch trace enough).

## Advanced notes

- **EPC URN** — `urn:epc:id:sgtin:GCP.itemRef.serial`.
- **Tag URI** — RFID encoding of SGTIN with binary form (96 bits).
- **AI (21)** — serial in classic AI element string.
- **AI (10)** — batch/lot (bulk level; NOT serial).
- **AI (254)** — GLN extension component.
- **SSCC serial** — 17-char (GCP + serial reference).
- **GIAI / GRAI** — asset serials.
- **Serial pool** — pre-generated blocks awaiting use; audit for shrinkage.
- **Reprint recovery** — new serial + parent-child link to invalidated one.
- **Regulator-specific formats** — CDSCO adds encryption + mandatory reporting timing.
- **Analytics** — issue-vs-dispense ratio; unusual gaps trigger investigation.
- **Reserved ranges** — some brands reserve serial prefixes for pilot / production / recall test.
